reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When modeling probabilities or neural networks, we often need to take any real number—ranging from negative infinity to positive infinity—and map it neatly into a probability between zero and one. Linear functions fail here because they grow without bound. Instead, mathematicians turn to the logistic function, a classic sigmoid curve that smoothly bends inputs into this restricted range.

At the heart of the logistic function is the exponential term $e^{-k(x - x_0)}$. As the input $x$ grows large and positive, this term vanishes, driving the denominator to one and the output to one. As $x$ drops toward negative infinity, the exponential dominates, pushing the denominator upward and driving the output down toward zero.

By adjusting the steepness $k$ and the midpoint $x_0$, we can control how abruptly the transition happens. The derivative reveals that the maximum rate of change occurs right at the midpoint, dropping off symmetrically as we move away. This elegant squashing mechanism makes the sigmoid indispensable for turning continuous scores into reliable binary decisions.
